title: Parking Lot Concurrency & Testing
description: Thread-safe spot allocation using CAS vs locks, comprehensive unit testing strategy, integration tests, and stress testing concurrent parking operations.

segments.text: Two cars arrive simultaneously at the last available spot. Without thread safety, both get assigned the same spot. In a real parking system, this means a collision. Thread-safe spot allocation is not optional. The choice between locks and lock-free CAS operations has distinct performance and correctness tradeoffs.

The lock-based approach: acquire a mutex before checking and assigning a spot. Simple and correct, but creates a bottleneck. If one thousand cars arrive per minute, the lock serializes all operations. Throughput degrades linearly. The critical section must be minimal — lock, read, write, unlock. Never do I/O while holding a lock.

Compare-And-Swap is lock-free. Read the spot status — available. Attempt CAS from available to occupied atomically. If another thread changed it first, CAS fails and you try the next spot. No locks, no blocking, but potential starvation under extreme contention. Java AtomicReference and C++ std atomic both support CAS natively.

Use a ConcurrentLinkedQueue of spot IDs — poll returns and removes an available spot atomically. Returning a car offers the spot back. This eliminates the search-then-assign race entirely. For typed spots — compact, regular, handicapped — maintain separate queues per type with overflow logic between queues.

Your parking lot has a VIP section. When VIP spots fill, VIP cars overflow to regular spots. Regular cars never take VIP spots. How would you implement this priority-based allocation with thread safety?
segments.thought_prompt: Design thread-safe spot allocation with VIP overflow to regular spots but not vice versa.

segments.text: Unit tests should cover: park successfully, park when full returns error, wrong vehicle type fails, unpark returns correct car, double-unpark fails, capacity tracking is accurate. Each test must be independent and deterministic — no shared mutable state between tests. Mock the spot selection strategy for isolation.

Integration tests verify components work together. Park multiple cars across floors and types, verify capacity decreases correctly, unpark some and verify spots are reusable, test the full entry-to-exit payment flow. Use a real database if your design persists state — in-memory H2 for speed, PostgreSQL for production fidelity.

Stress test concurrent access: spin up one hundred threads trying to park and unpark rapidly. Assert total parked never exceeds capacity. Assert no spot is double-assigned. Run for sixty seconds and verify invariants hold. Use a CountDownLatch to synchronize thread starts for maximum contention. This catches race conditions unit tests miss.

Define system invariants: parked count plus available count equals total capacity. No spot appears in both occupied and available sets simultaneously. Every parked car has a valid entry timestamp. These invariants should be checkable in O(1) time and verified after every operation in debug builds.
Your stress test reveals one in ten thousand park operations takes over five hundred milliseconds due to CAS retry loops. Is this acceptable for a real parking garage? How would you mitigate it?
segments.thought_prompt: CAS retries cause 500ms tail latency under extreme load. Accept it or fix it?

segments.text: Thread-safe parking lot design uses CAS for lock-free allocation or locks for simplicity, concurrent queues for O(1) spot assignment, and comprehensive testing at three levels: unit for correctness, integration for component interaction, stress for concurrency. The testing strategy is as important as the implementation — concurrency bugs are invisible until production.
